A.title: CASE A — THE SHARED FOLDER
A.description: A company’s staff noticed odd behaviour on their computers after someone opened a document from a shared folder. The IT team has pulled the file’s details and a log of what happened on one affected computer. You are the investigators.
A.guide: What you’re given: Exhibit A shows the file properties; Exhibit B logs programs starting, network connections and scheduled tasks; Exhibit C contains notes about normal activity. How to read it: Each log line has a time, the program that acted and what it did. “Started” means one program launched another, so follow the chain one step at a time. An address such as 185.220.0.14:443 is a remote address and port. What you’ll be asked: identify the real file type, follow the process chain, spot when malware persistence was created, and choose the first containment step. Watch out for: activity that looks normal but is not. Check each line before trusting its name.
exhibits:
Displayed name   Annual_Report.pdf
Icon             PDF
Size             2 KB
Opens with       Windows Shell
Exhibit B — process and network log

09:41:02 explorer.exe (4120) started cmd.exe (5510)
09:41:03 cmd.exe (5510) started powershell.exe (5522) -w hidden -enc JAB...
09:41:05 powershell.exe (5522) connected to 185.220.0.14:443
09:43:20 schtasks.exe created task "WinUpdateCheck" (run at logon) -> C:\Users\Public\upd.exe
09:43:21 upd.exe connected to 185.220.0.14:443
10:05:00 chrome.exe connected to 142.250.80.46:443
10:12:00 backup.exe wrote 4 GB to \\NAS01\backup
The backup job and the browser traffic are normal.

questions.q: What is the real file type of “Annual_Report.pdf”?
questions.hint: Ask whether a multi-page report fits in a couple of kilobytes.
Follow who started whom, one step at a time.

questions.q: At what time did the attacker make sure the malware survives a restart?
questions.hint: Look for the line that schedules something to run at logon.

questions.q: What is the first containment step that keeps evidence in memory intact?
questions.hint: Evidence in memory disappears when power is lost.

B.title: CASE B — THE STUDENT PORTAL
B.description: The student portal slowed down for about two minutes one morning. Someone checked the web server’s log and noticed unusual requests. You are the incident response team.
B.guide: What you’re given: Exhibit A is the web server request log; Exhibit B contains other notes, some of which may not matter. How to read it: Each line shows a time, the request and the result. 200 means success, 500 means the server hit an error, and rows= shows how many database records came back. In a web address, %20 is a space and %27 is an apostrophe. What you’ll be asked: find the first hostile request, identify the attack, name the keyword that attached another table’s data, and give the coding practice that prevents it. Watch out for: the same character can be harmless. Compare the server response, not just the character.
exhibits:
10:01:40 GET /search?name=O%27Brien                                200
10:02:11 GET /courses?id=12                                        200
10:02:19 GET /courses?id=12&sort=name                              200
10:02:26 GET /static/logo.png                                      200
10:02:30 GET /courses?id=12%27                                     500
10:02:44 GET /courses?id=12%20OR%201%3D1                           200  rows=4800
10:03:02 GET /courses?id=12%20UnIoN%20SeLeCt%20username,password%20FrOm%20users  200
10:05:10 POST /login user=asha                                     200
Server load stayed normal, and the certificate expires next month.

questions.q: At what time did the first hostile request arrive?
questions.hint: The same character can be harmless. Compare what the server did with it each time.

questions.q: What type of attack is this?
questions.hint: Decode the % codes and read what was added after id=12.

questions.q: Which keyword at 10:03:02 attached data from another table?
questions.hint: It combines the results of two SELECT queries.

questions.q: Which ONE coding practice removes the root cause?
questions.hint: The fix stops user input from ever being treated as SQL.

C.title: CASE C — THE CONFERENCE WI-FI
C.description: After a conference, accounts were used from another city. The security team collected a scan of the Wi-Fi at the venue, the certificate shown on a login page and the company’s sign-in log. You are the investigators.
C.guide: What you’re given: Exhibit A shows the Wi-Fi networks visible at the conference; Exhibit B shows the certificate on a login page; Exhibit C is the sign-in log; Exhibit D is a note that may not matter. How to read it: WPA2 means a network needs a password, while Open means it does not. A certificate states which website it was issued to, so compare that with the page address. Read the sign-in log in time order and compare the cities. What you’ll be asked: identify the certificate domain, find whose account was used first from the unfamiliar city, name the wireless attack, and say how to remove an attacker who is already signed in. Watch out for: two things that look identical but are not. Compare line by line.
exhibits: Exhibit A — Wi-Fi scan at the conference

SSID             Security   Signal
CORPORATE_GUEST  WPA2-Pers  -70
CORPORATE_GUEST  Open       -38
Exhibit B — certificate shown on the login page

Page address     login.company.com
Issued to        login-company-secure.net
Issued by        Unknown (self-signed)
Valid from       today

14:02:10 amit  OK    ip=10.40.5.22   city=Chennai
14:05:44 sana  OK    ip=10.40.5.31   city=Chennai
14:09:03 amit  OK    ip=185.220.9.7  city=Bucharest
14:11:30 sana  OK    ip=185.220.9.7  city=Bucharest
15:20:00 ravi  FAIL  ip=10.40.5.40   city=Chennai
15:20:08 ravi  OK    ip=10.40.5.40   city=Chennai

questions.q: In Exhibit B, which domain was the certificate actually issued to?
questions.hint: Read the “Issued to” line character by character.

questions.q: Whose account was used from the unfamiliar city first?
questions.hint: Order the log by time, not by who complained first.

questions.q: Name the wireless attack shown in Exhibit A.
questions.hint: Two networks share one name, and only one asks for no password.

questions.q: Beyond resetting passwords, which action cuts off an attacker who is already signed in?
questions.hint: Changing the lock does not remove someone already inside.
